description:
Wesam Saad introduces Fundamentals of the Faith as an interactive course intended to bring theology into everyday life. Before beginning the first lesson, he asks participants what they hope to learn and which doctrines they find difficult. His commitment is to help every student understand, rather than simply deliver information. Questions, discussion and patient explanation will therefore shape the course, with individual lessons extending across several meetings when needed.

The introduction sets out three aims: seeing unbelievers come to faith, helping believers grow, and equipping Christians for ministry. Drawing on 1 Peter 2:2, Matthew 28 and Ephesians 4:11–12, Wesam connects learning with spiritual growth and teaching others. He warns that impressive theological knowledge can coexist with pride and damaged relationships. Understanding should instead produce humility, love for God, patience and costly obedience to Christ.

Practical preparation includes listening to the suggested sermons, answering workbook questions and using optional quizzes to identify misunderstandings. These activities serve learning rather than merely completing a book. Participants are encouraged to invest effort, ask questions and consider how each doctrine should change their worship, conduct and service at home and in the church.

questions.question: What are the three main purposes of the course?
questions.answer: Wesam wants unbelievers to hear the gospel and come to faith, believers to grow in holiness, and Christians to be equipped to serve and teach others. The course is intended to reach the heart and shape life, rather than supply information alone.

questions.question: Why does the introduction warn against knowledge without changed character?
questions.answer: Wesam describes people who can explain theology impressively while their relationships are marked by pride and conflict. He wants understanding of God to produce humility, love, patience, gentleness and willingness to sacrifice for Christ.

questions.question: How does 1 Peter 2:2 shape the teacher’s approach?
questions.answer: The image of newborn babies longing for milk expresses the desire for spiritual growth through God’s word. Wesam also uses it to explain his responsibility to make the material understandable to every participant.

questions.question: What place will interaction have in these studies?
questions.answer: Participants are encouraged to ask questions, think through biblical answers and discuss what they are learning. Wesam intends to facilitate that process rather than turn every meeting into a lecture, allowing time for difficult issues and practical application.

questions.question: How are participants encouraged to prepare?
questions.answer: They can listen to the suggested sermon, take notes, bring questions and complete the workbook beforehand. Wesam explains that class time is for developing and discussing the material, and that greater preparation will generally help participants gain more from it.

questions.question: What are the workbook correction and quizzes intended to achieve?
questions.answer: They give participants feedback about what they have understood and where they need correction. Wesam offers to return corrected answers, and presents participation in the quizzes as an aid to growth rather than a compulsory requirement.

questions.question: Why is one lesson expected to require several sessions?
questions.answer: A lesson covers a substantial topic, while a session is one meeting. Working through questions, testing understanding and considering application together takes time. The aim is that students learn and live the truth, rather than simply finish a lesson at each gathering.

questions.question: How should learning lead to ministry beyond the class?
questions.answer: Wesam connects the course with Ephesians 4 and the command to make disciples. Christians should be able to pass on what they learn to their families and others, helping people come to faith and grow in the Lord rather than keeping the teaching to themselves.
